facts: In 2023, between 20 and 70 cm of snow fell at the end of April in areas such as Dalarna, Värmland, Västernorrland and Jämtland. Such adverse weather conditions can lead to unsuccessful nesting.

According to the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, a total of 498.5 occupied golden eagle territories were reported in Sweden in 2023. Of these, 166 nestings resulted in fledging chicks, which is the lowest number of successful nestings since 2018.
The highest number of occupied territories was recorded in Gotland since the inventories began, indicating a positive trend for the golden eagle on the island.

The golden eagle avoids areas of human activity and requires undisturbed nesting sites. Disturbance near nests, especially during the breeding season, can lead to failed nests. Lack of suitable nesting trees and reduced availability of prey, such as gallinaceous birds and hares, also pose threats to the species.

To protect the golden eagle, it is important to identify and preserve nest sites. More than 80 percent of nests are on state land, and about 40 percent of them are located in nature conservation areas. In forestry areas, forestry activities near nests are prohibited during the breeding season to minimize disturbance.

Geese are increasing explosively, and so is the damage to agriculture. According to LRF's calculations, geese caused damage worth approximately SEK 130 million in 2023, which is an increase of more than 50 percent compared to 2020. At the same time, there is much evidence that interest in goose hunting is decreasing among hunters. It is an equation that does not add up.

Interest in goose hunting also seems to have cooled down. There are probably several reasons for this. Greylag geese and perhaps especially barnacle geese are much more difficult to hunt than the now, at least in Skåne, much rarer Canada geese.

A warmer climate is affecting nature in Sweden. The average migratory bird now returns up to ten days earlier than it did 30–40 years ago. This can affect competition between species and their adaptation to new conditions.

Several goose species have increased significantly in Sweden in recent decades. This has led to problems for both bathers and farmers. Research is underway to understand the reasons for the increase and to find solutions to the conflicts that arise.

In a study, 176 live greylag geese were captured, ringed, and X-rayed with a portable X-ray machine before being released. And the findings give rise to concern. One in five geese had between 1 and 16 shotgun pellets encapsulated in their bodies.

One explanation may be that the decrease is a result of a new inventory methodology for wolverines introduced in 2013. Further research is needed to ascertain whether changes and trends are linked to changes in inventory methodology or whether there is a real decrease in the number of wolverines that could be due to, for example, increased protective hunting.
Up to 9 out of 10 wolverines die in Sweden's extensive illegal hunting
Svensk Jakt reports on extensive hunting of wolverines in the border areas, where the targets for shooting are far above the estimated annual growth.

Over the investigated period, 28 suspected cases of golden eagle poaching were reported, of which two cases were dropped during investigation. In ten of the reports, no preliminary investigation was initiated because the chance of finding the perpetrator was considered too small. Most of the reports are from people who have found a dead golden eagle, either intact or in pieces.

We have found 49 reports of suspected unlawful hunting of wolverines between the years 1995–2005, of which 6 cases have been dropped during investigation. For wolverines, too, the dark figure is vary large. If we compare 43 reported substantial suspicions over 11 years, with the researchers calculations of 50 poached wolverines in the past year it becomes evident that a substantial proportion of these crimes are never detected.
